top_line: Taiwan counted votes today in local elections Beijing watched closely, while Spain heads into Sunday's vote that could put the far right in national government for the first time since Franco.

ai_roundup.title: Israel fast-tracks AI data centres, calling them a national-security priority
ai_roundup.summary: Israel is speeding up approvals for AI data centres, including a major facility near Ashdod, after classifying them as national infrastructure to bypass local permitting rules, Al Jazeera reports. Prime Minister Netanyahu framed the push as a security imperative, arguing a "small and threatened country" must control its own computing power. The Israel Electrical Authority has already capped new capacity at 200MW amid strained grid demand.

ai_roundup.title: Russia's AI ambitions are faltering under the weight of the war
ai_roundup.summary: Russia's push for AI supremacy is stalling, the New York Times reports from a Moscow AI conference. Western sanctions have cut Russian imports of GPUs and other AI-critical chips by roughly 84% since before the invasion, while skilled engineers have fled the country in waves. Analysts say Moscow is growing increasingly dependent on Chinese hardware and expertise to offset the shortfall, with no clear way to close the gap soon.

ai_roundup.title: Child safety becomes a flashpoint in Spain's election as TikTok faces scrutiny
ai_roundup.summary: Investigators at Fundación Maldita.es found more than 1,100 TikTok videos containing child sexual abuse material with roughly 48 million views, and flagged about 26,000 accounts potentially linked to predators, Tech Policy Press reports. Madrid prosecutors filed a complaint against TikTok's Spanish subsidiary; the European Commission is separately examining the platform's compliance with the Digital Services Act ahead of Sunday's election.

ai_roundup.title: Ladybird browser ships its first alpha, built with no Chromium code
ai_roundup.summary: Ladybird, an independent browser engine written from scratch by SerenityOS creator Andreas Kling's team, released its first downloadable alpha for macOS and Linux, Ars Technica reports. Unlike Chrome, Firefox, or Safari, it shares no code with existing browsers, aiming to break the web's near-total dependence on Chromium. Early reviewers called the build surprisingly capable, though it remains unfinished and aimed at developers for now.

ai.title: Do We Need a Right to Reality?
ai.author: Jacobo Castellanos and Bruna Santos
ai.why: As generative AI makes convincing fake video, audio and documents trivial to produce, these WITNESS researchers ask a sharper question than most AI-ethics pieces: not whether deepfakes are bad, but whether democracies need an entirely new right -- to know how content was made, not to be impersonated, not to be deceived at scale -- to protect the shared basis for truth-finding that courts, journalism and elections all depend on.

mind.title: Why Anything Exists
mind.author: Andrew T Brenner
mind.why: A philosopher takes on the oldest question there is -- why anything exists at all -- and argues 'nothing' was never as simple as Leibniz assumed, since a world with nothing in it would still contain truths about logic, math and morality. A genuine break from the news cycle that rewards slow, careful reasoning over hot takes.

paper.title: The Fabric of AI Governance
paper.author: Tommaso Giardini and Nils Deeg
paper.why: Rather than another country-by-country survey, this report maps AI rules by concern -- transparency, safety, bias, labour, IP -- across 84 domestic laws and nine international frameworks, showing where regulators agree (disclosure and risk assessment lead) and where they still diverge. A genuinely useful structure for a non-technical reader trying to track a fast-fragmenting regulatory landscape.

media.title: Is Anthropic on the Cusp of RSI? Inside the Redacted METR Report
media.author: Luisa Rodriguez
media.why: METR spent 11 weeks inside Anthropic and estimated its AI is now speeding up its own research roughly twice as fast as a year ago -- brushing against Anthropic's own 'two years of progress in one' safety threshold. Rodriguez walks through what METR could verify, the strongest reasons it might be wrong, and why Anthropic's heavy redactions leave the public unable to check the claim itself.

concept_ai.term: What is RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback)?
paragraphs: Most large language models start as next-word predictors, trained to guess likely text from the internet -- a process that makes them fluent but not necessarily helpful, honest or safe. RLHF is the technique labs use to close that gap. Human raters compare pairs of model responses to the same prompt and say which they prefer; those preferences train a separate "reward model" to predict what humans will like. The base model is then fine-tuned with reinforcement learning to maximize that reward model's score, nudging it toward answers people actually want rather than merely plausible ones.

RLHF is why a raw pretrained model can ramble or refuse nothing in particular, while the chatbot built on top of it mostly follows instructions and declines harmful requests. It's also why model behavior reflects the particular humans who did the rating -- their preferences, blind spots and cultural assumptions get baked in as "alignment." The technique has real limits: human feedback is slow and expensive to collect at scale, and models can learn to exploit the reward model's quirks rather than genuinely improve, a failure researchers call "reward hacking."
concept_ai.why: Why it matters: RLHF is the main lever labs use to make raw AI capability match human values and expectations -- which is exactly why fights over whose values get encoded, and how robust that alignment really is, sit at the center of today's AI safety debates.

big_moves.headline: Mercor raises $750M Series D, doubling its valuation to $20B in just over a year
big_moves.who: Nvidia, Salesforce, Benchmark, Felicis, General Catalyst and others -> Mercor, an AI training-data and evaluation startup (Nov 10)
big_moves.why: The round, double Mercor's valuation from its October 2025 raise, shows how much capital is still chasing the "picks and shovels" labor layer that helps AI labs test, evaluate and refine their models, even as broader AI funding cools for the holidays.

big_moves.headline: Stanford AI researchers launch Noeri with $110M to build "self-improving" enterprise AI
big_moves.who: Menlo Ventures (lead), with Madrona, Kindred, Wing, NEA and strategic backing from Nvidia, Cisco and Snowflake -> Noeri, founded by Stanford's Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin (Nov 16)
big_moves.why: The bet is that AI systems which keep adapting after deployment -- rather than freezing once training ends -- are the next competitive edge, and that top academic AI safety researchers, not just frontier labs, can build that commercially.

geo_roundup.title: Taiwan counts votes in elections Beijing is watching closely
geo_roundup.summary: Taiwan held "nine-in-one" local elections Saturday, with early tallies showing KMT incumbent Chiang Wan-an leading DPP challenger Puma Shen for Taipei mayor, Al Jazeera and The Print report. China has called Shen, a vocal Beijing critic, wanted for "separatism." Taiwan's defense ministry counted roughly 33 Chinese military aircraft sorties over the two days of voting, part of what officials call a pressure campaign.

geo_roundup.title: Ukraine's long-range strikes inside Russia keep growing in scale and reach
geo_roundup.summary: Ukraine's deep-strike campaign is expanding, the New York Times reports, with drones now hitting refineries, defense plants and military sites hundreds of kilometers inside Russia. Kyiv says the campaign has cost Russia billions in oil-export losses and plans to expand its deep-strike units further, even as Moscow steps up its own drone and missile barrages on Ukrainian cities.

geo_roundup.title: Israeli strike kills two Doctors Without Borders staff at Gaza clinic
geo_roundup.summary: An Israeli strike killed two Doctors Without Borders watchmen at a Gaza City clinic the group says was clearly marked and known to Israeli forces, raising its Gaza death toll to 17, Al Jazeera reports. Israel's military claimed without evidence that the men were Hamas fighters. WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the strike "outrageous and unacceptable."

geo_roundup.title: Costa Rica releases UN rapporteur Albanese after court intervenes
geo_roundup.summary: Costa Rica released UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese from a second night's detention at a San José airport after the country's Constitutional Court ordered her release, Al Jazeera reports. Costa Rica had cited an "international alert" over alleged terrorism links, which Albanese -- already under US sanctions over her Gaza advocacy -- called "a disgrace." She had been traveling to receive an honorary doctorate.

geo_roundup.title: Yemen's government forces strike Houthis as UN warns of worsening hunger
geo_roundup.summary: Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces struck Houthi positions as the UN warned Yemen faces some of the world's worst hunger, with 1.8 million people in government-held areas at emergency levels, Al Jazeera reports. Aid groups blame deep donor cuts, including from the US, for worsening the crisis; renewed fighting has displaced over 300,000 people and pushed up food and fuel prices.

geo_concept.title: Concept in Review: Spain's Far Right, From Franco to Vox
paragraphs: When Francisco Franco died in 1975 after 36 years of dictatorship, Spain's political class made a deliberate choice: rather than prosecute the old regime, they negotiated a transition built on what's often called a "pact of forgetting." The 1978 constitution restored democracy and devolved power to Spain's regions, but left Francoist-era elites largely untouched and shelved any open reckoning with the dictatorship's crimes. For decades afterward, the far right barely registered at the ballot box -- explicitly Francoist parties won only a handful of seats, and mainstream conservatives absorbed most right-wing voters under the Popular Party (PP), founded in 1989 partly by former Franco-era officials.

Vox split off from the PP in 2013-14, initially over the PP's handling of Catalonia's push for independence, and for years remained a fringe outfit. The 2017 Catalan independence crisis changed that: Vox's hard line on national unity, immigration and cultural issues -- paired with Europe's broader populist wave -- helped it win its first seats in Andalusia's 2018 regional election, then enter national parliament in 2019, the first far-right party to do so since the transition. It has since become Spain's third-largest party, with a young, online-savvy base.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called Sunday's snap election after parliament rejected his renter-protection measures, betting voters would reward eight years of social-policy gains. Polls instead show the PP winning the most seats but needing Vox to reach a 176-seat majority -- a combination that would put the far right in national government for the first time since Franco's dictatorship ended. The campaign has also been shaped by a TikTok child-safety scandal and corruption allegations swirling around Sánchez's inner circle, giving Vox fresh openings on both law-and-order and tech-platform accountability.

world.title: Spain heads into Sunday's election a country divided over Sánchez's record
world.summary: Spain votes Sunday in a snap election pitting supporters of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's social-policy record against a conservative PP-Vox bloc, which polls show winning the most seats but needing Vox to reach a majority, Al Jazeera reports. That combination would mark the far right's first time in national government since Franco. The campaign has also turned on immigration, corruption allegations and a deadly train-crash controversy.

world.title: Explosion beside Afghan school kills at least six students
world.summary: At least six students died and 97 people were injured when an explosion tore through a house storing dynamite beside a middle school in Afghanistan's Kunar province, Al Jazeera reports. Officials said the toll was preliminary and blamed "negligence and carelessness" by miners who were using the house to store explosives near the school.

world.title: Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie convicted over 123 starvation deaths
world.summary: A Kenyan court convicted cult leader Paul Mackenzie of manslaughter over the starvation deaths of 123 followers, Al Jazeera reports. Mackenzie, whose case shocked Kenya after mass graves were found in 2023, is already serving a 200-year sentence for murdering nearly 200 children tied to the same group, adding to a broader reckoning over Kenya's oversight of religious movements.

world.title: FIFA may scrap the Peace Prize it gave Trump
world.summary: FIFA may scrap the Peace Prize it awarded Donald Trump last December, the New York Times reports, after council members pushed president Gianni Infantino amid criticism that the award politicized football. The governing body's football social-responsibility committee will now decide whether to reform or drop the prize, which critics called a consolation gift after Trump missed out on the Nobel Peace Prize.

world.title: Canada's top court upholds Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public workers
world.summary: Canada's Supreme Court ruled that Quebec may keep its ban on public employees such as teachers, judges and police wearing religious symbols on the job, the New York Times reports. The law, Bill 21, has drawn years of legal challenges from religious and civil-liberties groups and relies on the constitutional "notwithstanding clause," which Quebec must renew every five years.

world.title: Johannesburg lawmakers snub Helen Zille's bid to become mayor
world.summary: Johannesburg's new city council snubbed Helen Zille's bid to become mayor, the New York Times reports, after weeks of coalition wrangling between her Democratic Alliance, the ANC and ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba, who had refused to back her. Zille, a veteran opposition figure, said she would instead lead the council's opposition benches rather than broker a deal that kept her out.

india.title: INDIA bloc hardens opposition to delimitation bill as DMK breaks ranks to back it
india.summary: India's opposition INDIA bloc formally decided to oppose the government's delimitation bill as "anti-SC/ST" and a threat to democracy, even as bloc member DMK announced support for the Centre's proposal, The Hindu reports, days before a special Parliament session convenes on November 30. Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge called the bill "dangerous"; critics including Arundhati Roy argue it is really about gerrymandering, not women's representation.

india.title: India declares Kashmir free of homegrown militants, but analysts say insurgency has adapted
india.summary: India's Home Minister declared Kashmir free of homegrown militants after Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Mohammad Lateef Bhat was killed on November 18, calling it the first such milestone since 1989, Al Jazeera reports. Analysts and former officials say the insurgency has simply changed form, pointing to rebranded groups, "hybrid militants" who evade official lists, and a shift in violence toward the forests of Jammu, where 33 people have died since 2021.

india.title: Varanasi set for two elevated highway corridors along the Ganga and Varuna
india.summary: Varanasi is set to get two elevated corridors spanning nearly 89 km along the Ganga and Varuna rivers, part of a roughly ₹25,446 crore project the Cabinet cleared earlier this year, the Indian Express reports. The Ganga corridor includes a 910-metre cable-stayed bridge; officials say the projects should cut cross-city travel time from about 60 minutes to 20 once complete.

india.title: Student suicides at India's elite IITs expose gaps in campus mental-health support
india.summary: Al Jazeera examines a wave of student suicides at India's IITs, where alumni groups and a Supreme Court-appointed task force have documented dozens of deaths in recent years, with a disproportionate share among SC, ST and OBC students. The task force's interim findings cite inadequate faculty mental-health training and deep student isolation on hostel campuses; its final report is still months away.

know.headline: Europe's Hera spacecraft reveals the aftermath of humanity's first asteroid-deflection test
know.body: ESA's Hera probe returned its closest images yet of Dimorphos, the small asteroid NASA's DART mission deliberately crashed into in 2022, revealing boulders, craters and ridges reshaped by the impact. Hera will next carry out a close-range "crash site investigation" using multiple instruments to measure how much the collision actually altered the asteroid's orbit and structure.

writing.connection_question: WITNESS's "right to reality" piece argues democracies need new protections against AI-generated deception -- including a right to know how content was made and not be deceived at scale. The METR/80,000 Hours deep dive into Anthropic's AI R&D report raises a structurally similar problem about AI labs themselves: Anthropic redacted most of the evidence METR found most convincing about how fast its AI is accelerating its own research, so the public can't independently verify whether Anthropic has crossed its own safety threshold. Should the obligation to make extraordinary claims verifiable -- whether it's a deepfake's origin or a lab's self-reported capability jump -- rest on the same principle? Who should hold that verification power -- regulators, outside auditors like METR, journalists -- and what happens when the companies being checked are also the ones funding the checking?
